top_choice_rationale: P002 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) credits a mature framework of about 25 to 30 years that made electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity objects of formal analysis with testable predictions about fiscal policy. Credit is concentrated and can be bounded: Persson and Tabellini for the constitutions and electoral-rules programme, Besley for the separable state-capacity strand, with Persson and Tabellini alone as a defensible fallback. The main weaknesses are the weaker cross-country identification and the neighbouring 2024 institutions prize, so the citation should rest on the framework and not on settled causal estimates. P001 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) is a close second. It has the broader policy reach and, under an originating-ideas criterion, separable roles. But it leaves out estimation-side contributors with serious claims, the Taylor rule's status as science or prescription is unresolved, and the Fischer and Phelps priority questions remain open. P003 (Helpman, Melitz) is a clean two-name case with direct firm-level tests, but credit for the empirical pioneers and the 2008 trade prize lineage weigh against it. No award is last because all three proposals describe mature, identifiable contributions. This judgement rests on the supplied files and general knowledge, not on independent verification.
